title: Ethiopian Amete Mihret Calendar
intro: The Ethiopian calendar is a living calendar used in Ethiopia. It divides the year into thirteen months, follows a leap-year rhythm and numbers its years differently from the Gregorian calendar.
summary: Twelve 30-day months plus Pagume, a short thirteenth month.
epoch: Amete Mihret means 'Years of Mercy'. Its Christian-era reckoning differs from the Gregorian era by roughly seven or eight years, depending on the date.
year_rule: The first twelve months each have thirty days. The last month, Pagume, has five days or six in a leap year. Ethiopian New Year generally falls on 11 or 12 September in the Gregorian calendar.
after_note: Meskerem begins the Ethiopian year in September, not January. For a real-world conversion, use both the year and the exact day.
history_heading: A CALENDAR STILL IN DAILY USE
history: Ethiopia preserves a calendar descended from the Alexandrian tradition. Its months shape civil, religious and everyday life, including New Year (Enkutatash). The Ethiopian Amete Mihret numbering must not be confused with the distinct Amete Alem era.
limits: The implementation is the Amete Mihret calendar and its leap cycle; it is not a general-purpose replacement for every Ethiopian historical era or the separate Ethiopian clock convention.
